content: Sesame oil, also known as gingelly oil or til oil, is an edible vegetable oil extracted from sesame seeds. It is widely used as a cooking oil in South India and as a flavor enhancer in Southeast Asian cuisine. Composition Sesame oil is composed of various fatty acids, which contribute to its unique properties and uses. Historical Context Sesame seeds were among the first crops processed for oil and used as condiments. The Tamil word for oil, ennai, originates from the Tamil words el (sesame) and nei (fat). Before 600 BC, the Assyrians utilized sesame oil as food, salve, and medicine, primarily among the wealthy due to its high cost. In Hindu culture, til oil is considered sacred and is used in votive lamps. Lighting a lamp filled with til oil in front of Lord Hanuman is believed to remove obstacles and difficulties in life. Nomenclature In Tamil, sesame oil is called Nalla Ennai, meaning good oil. In Telugu, it is referred to as Nuvvula Noona, and in Kannada, it is called Yellenne. It is also commonly known as gingelly oil in India. Manufacturing Process The extraction of sesame oil is not fully automated. Sesame seeds are encased in capsules that do not open until the seeds are fully ripe. Farmers manually harvest the plants, allow them to ripen further, and then extract the seeds. The discovery of a non-shattering mutant in 1943 led to efforts to develop high-yield, shatter-resistant varieties. Despite advancements, harvest losses due to shattering remain a challenge, limiting domestic production in the U.S. Sesame oil is relatively expensive due to global shortages. Varieties Sesame oil varies in color depending on its processing. Cold-pressed sesame oil is nearly colorless, Indian sesame oil is golden, and Chinese sesame oil is dark brown due to the use of toasted seeds. Cold-pressed oil has a milder flavor compared to toasted oil. Sesame oil is available in various forms, with cold-pressed oil commonly found in Western health shops, while hot-pressed varieties are preferred in most Asian countries. Uses Cooking Sesame oil is considered more stable than most vegetable oils due to its antioxidant content, making it less prone to rancidity. It has a high boiling point, allowing it to retain its natural structure even at high temperatures. It is widely used in Asia, particularly in Tamil Nadu, where its use is comparable to olive oil in the Mediterranean. Body Massage Sesame oil is reputed to penetrate the skin easily and is commonly used in India for oil massages. Hair Treatment Applying sesame oil to the hair is believed to darken it and reduce body heat, potentially preventing hair loss. It is also used for scalp massages. Food Manufacturing Sesame oil is used in the production of pickles and, in Western countries, refined sesame oil is used to make margarine. Drug Manufacturing Sesame oil is utilized in the preparation of Ayurvedic medicines. Worship In Hindu rituals, sesame oil is used in brass or silver lamps placed in front of deities and for performing puja in temples. Industrial Uses Industrially, sesame oil serves as a solvent in injected drugs or intravenous solutions, a carrier oil in cosmetics, and a coating for stored grains to prevent weevil infestations. It also exhibits synergy with certain insecticides. Alternative Medicine Vitamins and Minerals Sesame oil is a source of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps lower cholesterol. It also contains magnesium, copper, calcium, iron, zinc, and vitamin B6. Copper may alleviate rheumatoid arthritis, magnesium supports vascular and respiratory health, calcium helps prevent colon cancer, osteoporosis, migraines, and PMS, and zinc promotes bone health. Despite its richness in vitamin E, research on the medicinal properties of sesame oil is limited. Blood Pressure Sesame oil is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), which may help control blood pressure. It contains high levels of omega-6 fatty acids and natural preservatives like sesamol and sesamin, making it unique among oils. Studies suggest that PUFAs and sesamin in sesame oil may reduce blood pressure and inhibit cholesterol synthesis and absorption. Oil Pulling Sesame oil is one of the few oils recommended for oil pulling, an alternative oral health practice. Stress and Tension Sesame oil contains antioxidants and compounds with antidepressant properties. Proponents claim it helps combat senile changes, promotes well-being, and alleviates anxiety, nerve and bone disorders, poor circulation, and lowered immunity. It is also believed to relieve lethargy, fatigue, and insomnia while enhancing strength and vitality. General Claims Sesame oil is reputed to have therapeutic uses, including easing pain and muscle spasms, such as sciatica, dysmenorrhea, colic, backache, and joint pain. It is also believed to slow aging, promote longevity, and alleviate dryness both externally and internally. Some suggest it can relieve menopausal dryness, restore skin moisture, and ease symptoms like irritating coughs, cracking joints, and hard stools. However, these claims lack sufficient medical evidence. Adverse Effects Sesame oil is generally safe when consumed in recommended doses, but its long-term effects are not well-studied. Caution is advised for children, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and individuals with liver or kidney disease. Due to its laxative effects, it should be avoided by those with diarrhea. The American Heart Association recommends limiting polyunsaturated fats, such as those in sesame oil, to no more than 10% of total caloric intake. Sesame oil massage should be avoided after enemas, emetics, or purgatives, during the early stages of fever, or in cases of indigestion. People allergic to peanuts may also be more susceptible to sesame allergies, which can lead to severe reactions like anaphylactic shock. Those with sesame seed allergies should exercise caution when using sesame oil.
